name: Vitamin D

lead: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin made in the skin on exposure to ultraviolet B light and obtained from oily fish, fortified foods and supplements. It is essential for calcium absorption and bone health and is taken up by hair follicle cells that carry vitamin D receptors.

Low levels have been reported in several hair-loss conditions, including telogen effluvium and alopecia areata, but a causal role is unproven. Confirmed deficiency is treated with supplementation, whereas supplementation in people with normal levels has limited evidence of hair benefit.

paras: The active form, calcitriol, binds the vitamin D receptor, which is expressed in follicle keratinocytes and is needed for normal follicle cycling, particularly the return to the growth phase. The receptor also influences immune function, which may explain links to autoimmune hair loss.

Excess supplementation can cause hypercalcaemia, kidney stones and kidney damage, mostly with very high doses over long periods. Large trials in the general population have not shown major benefits for outcomes such as cancer and cardiovascular disease. Supplements are over the counter, and deficiency is confirmed by a blood test.

lead: Vitamin D is a group of fat-soluble secosteroid compounds, chiefly vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) and vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol), whose best-established role is increasing intestinal absorption of calcium and supporting bone health [1][2]. It is only conditionally essential in the diet, because the skin can synthesise cholecalciferol when exposed to ultraviolet B (UVB) light; it is also obtained from oily fish, egg yolks, fortified foods such as milk and cereals, and supplements [1][2].

In appearance-focused discussion, vitamin D is mostly raised in connection with hair. Low blood levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D have been reported in people with some hair-loss conditions, including telogen effluvium and alopecia areata, and hair-follicle cells carry the vitamin D receptor. Whether low vitamin D causes hair loss, and whether supplementing people with normal levels changes hair outcomes, has not been established by published trials.

Deficiency is common worldwide and is diagnosed by measuring serum 25(OH)D [1][3]. Supplementation reliably prevents and treats rickets, whereas the effects on many non-skeletal outcomes remain uncertain; a large randomised trial of vitamin D in the general population (VITAL) did not find reduced rates of invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events [1][4]. Excess intake from high-dose supplements can cause hypercalcaemia and related harms [1]. Vitamin D is sold over the counter as a supplement in most countries.

paras: Vitamin D supplementation is a reliable method for preventing and treating rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, and is used in people with or at risk of deficiency [1]. Clinical guidelines address evaluation, treatment and prevention of deficiency in at-risk groups [5]. Daily dosing regimens are generally described as having advantages over large weekly or monthly bolus doses for correcting deficiency, although consensus on optimal type, dose and duration is lacking [1].

Within hair-loss discussion, vitamin D is mentioned as a nutrient whose deficiency may accompany conditions such as telogen effluvium and alopecia areata, and some people take supplements on that basis. The vitamin D receptor is expressed in hair-follicle keratinocytes and is implicated in follicle cycling, and the vitamin also affects immune function, which has been proposed as relevant to autoimmune hair loss. These associations are observational; supplementing people who have normal levels has little supporting evidence for hair benefit.

More than a billion people worldwide are estimated to be deficient, with the reported proportion depending on the serum threshold used; a 2023 systematic review estimated roughly 15% of the global population falls below 30 nmol/L [1]. Deficiency occurs in the Middle East, Asia, Africa and South America as well as in North America and Europe, and is more prevalent in dark-skinned populations living at higher latitudes [1].

Causes include limited UVB exposure (high latitude, winter, indoor or urban living, clothing coverage, sunscreen use), ageing, chronic kidney disease and fat malabsorption [1]. Meta-analyses of observational studies have found that deficiency is more prevalent in people with obesity, in both adults and in children and adolescents [6][7]; an earlier clinical study reported decreased bioavailability of vitamin D in obesity [8]. Reviews describe deficiency as a widespread public-health problem requiring approaches to diagnosis, treatment and prevention [3][9].

Evidence on vitamin D comes from a very large literature, much of it outside appearance. The notes below summarise representative studies and reviews from the research record; none is a trial of vitamin D for hair growth or other cosmetic outcomes.

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 studies found lower serum 25(OH)D in people with psoriasis than in controls, but pooled randomised trials of oral supplementation (four trials, 173 treated patients) found no significant difference in Psoriasis Area and Severity Index scores at 3, 6 or 12 months [10]. A 2022 meta-analysis reported an association between deficiency and higher miscarriage risk (odds ratio 1.94 for deficient versus replete women) [11]. A 2022 systematic review of 19 intervention studies examined supplementation and sleep, with pre-post studies reporting improved sleep quality [12]. A 2023 meta-analysis of eight randomised trials (695 participants) reported lower primary dysmenorrhoea pain scores with vitamin D than placebo [13].

Randomised trials have also looked at supplementation in polycystic ovary syndrome (fertility markers and metabolic parameters), type 2 diabetes (metabolic and oxidative-stress markers over six months), endometriosis and dysmenorrhoea [14][15][16][17][18], and in women with recurrent implantation failure alongside vaginal probiotics [19]. These studies address reproductive and metabolic outcomes rather than appearance.

The VITAL randomised trial, which tested daily vitamin D3 supplementation in a large general-population sample, did not find a lower incidence of invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events than placebo [4]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials has also examined adverse events with long-term daily supplementation at 3,200 to 4,000 IU [20]. Registered trials include studies in pregnancy, lactation, multiple sclerosis, lupus, dialysis and neonatal sepsis [21][22][23][24][25][26].
No clinical trial specifically testing vitamin D supplementation for hair loss in people with normal vitamin D status is included in the research record for this entry.

Vitamin D toxicity (hypervitaminosis D) is described as rare. It has occurred historically with unregulated food fortification and more recently with inappropriate prescribing, non-prescribed use of very high-dose products, or manufacturing errors that put far more vitamin in a product than the label states [1]. It manifests mainly as hypercalcaemia, and long, high-dose exposure has been associated with kidney stones and kidney damage. Sunlight or tanning-bed exposure alone is not reported to cause toxicity, because skin synthesis is self-limiting [1].

Treatment of toxicity consists of stopping the supplement, with a low-calcium diet and sometimes corticosteroids; recovery is usually reported within about a month [1]. People with idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia, linked to a CYP24A1 mutation, are unusually sensitive to added vitamin D [1]. A label for one vitamin A, C and D paediatric product reports only rare allergic rash and advises keeping the product out of children's reach [27].

Cholecalciferol and ergocalciferol are converted in the liver to calcifediol (25-hydroxyvitamin D), the form measured to assess status, and then in the kidney and some immune cells to the active hormone calcitriol [1]. Calcitriol binds the vitamin D receptor, a nuclear receptor that acts as a transcription factor controlling genes for calcium-transport proteins such as TRPV6 and calbindin in the intestine [1]. Together with parathyroid hormone, this maintains calcium and phosphorus balance and supports bone [1].

The receptor is expressed in cells throughout the body, including immune cells and skin, and laboratory research has shown that vitamin D signalling can contribute to antimicrobial responses [28]. These broader effects are the basis for research interest in non-skeletal conditions, though trials of supplementation have mostly not confirmed clinical benefit for those outcomes [1].

The vitamin D forms are secosteroids, meaning one bond in the steroid ring system is broken. D2 and D3 differ in their side chains; D3 forms when ultraviolet light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin [1]. Some studies find D3 raises and sustains 25(OH)D more effectively, while others report equal efficacy for D2 [1].

In northern Europe, cod liver oil had a long folk-medicine history, and from the 1820s onward physicians observed that children given it did not develop rickets; giving children cod liver oil persisted into the 1950s [1]. Milk fortification with vitamin D began in the early 1930s [1]. The antirachitic factor was identified in the early 1920s, and the D2 and D3 forms were chemically characterised in 1931 and 1935 [1][2].

Vitamin D is among the most widely used supplements and is routinely mentioned in physique and health forums as part of a basic vitamin and mineral regimen, alongside discussion of blood-test checks for deficiency. Intake recommendations differ between bodies; the US Institute of Medicine's 2011 report set 600 IU daily for most adults and judged the evidence for many non-skeletal benefits inconclusive, while some researchers have argued that its conclusions were too definitive [1][29]. Because fortification, sun exposure and skin tone all affect status, public-health recommendations vary by country [1].
